title: Adaptive Local Measurements For Quantum Learning Can Exponentially Outperform Nonadaptive Global Measurements
authors: Alireza Goldar, Zhen Qin, Zhihui Zhu, Zhe-Xuan Gong, Michael B. Wakin
abstract: Can measurements chosen adaptively, in response to earlier outcomes, be exponentially more informative than measurements fixed in advance? In many quantum settings, adaptivity helps at most polynomially; known exponential advantages require coherent measurements across copies or restricted measurements. We show an exponential advantage measuring one copy at a time, with no quantum memory kept between state copies, even when the nonadaptive learner may perform arbitrary global measurements on each copy. We construct explicit families of multi-qubit states in which a scalar parameter is encoded in one of exponentially many candidate observables, with an auxiliary marker indicating which one. An adaptive protocol identifies the relevant observable and then measures it using only single-qubit measurements and one round of adaptation. At fixed accuracy, it needs logarithmically many copies as the qubit count grows, whereas every nonadaptive protocol needs exponentially many. The same mechanism yields an exponential gap in local asymptotic minimax mean squared error constants, tight up to the exponential base. The states are separable and classical in label-dependent product bases; no entanglement or other nonclassical correlations are required. The gap comes from measurement incompatibility: the candidate observables cannot be measured jointly, so a fixed measurement must divide its information budget among them, while adaptivity selects the informative one. Accordingly, the separation disappears when the candidate observables commute, and cannot occur with fully observed classical samples. Measurement incompatibility thus emerges as a resource for quantum learning, distinct from entanglement and quantum memory, that classical feedback alone can exploit.
summary: This work proves that adaptively choosing quantum measurements based on intermediate results can yield an exponential advantage in information gain over any fixed, nonadaptive measurement strategy. This advantage is shown to stem purely from the incompatibility of the candidate observables, requiring no entanglement or quantum memory. It establishes measurement incompatibility as a novel resource in quantum learning theory.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether adaptively chosen quantum measurements, based on previous outcomes, can provide an exponential advantage in information gain over measurements fixed in advance (nonadaptive global measurements).
main_result: An exponential advantage is demonstrated by showing that an adaptive protocol requires only logarithmically many copies, while the best nonadaptive protocol requires exponentially many copies, even for separable states.
method: The analysis uses Fisher information bounds to quantify the information gain, comparing the sample complexity required for adaptive versus nonadaptive estimation protocols.
model_or_system: The model involves multi-qubit states constructed with a 'marker register' and a 'signal register,' where an unknown scalar parameter is encoded in one of exponentially many candidate observables.
key_observables: Fisher information, Mean Squared Error (MSE), and the number of required measurement copies.
important_parameters: The separation scales are logarithmic ($\log n$) for adaptive vs. exponential ($2\Omega(n)$) for nonadaptive, where $n$ is the number of qubits.
main_assumptions: The separation relies fundamentally on the measurement incompatibility of the candidate observables, not on entanglement or quantum memory.
paper_structure: The paper develops the problem by first establishing the exponential advantage using a ternary construction, showing the advantage persists even when enlarging the measurement class to arbitrary product POVMs, and finally confirming the resource is measurement incompatibility.
why_interesting: It provides a fundamental resource theory result, showing that measurement incompatibility itself can be a resource for quantum learning, distinct from entanglement, which is highly relevant for understanding measurement limitations in complex quantum systems.
